concepts.text: Living organisms share defining features such as growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response to surroundings (background only; the 'What is Living?' section is deleted)
Exercise type: explain why growth and reproduction alone cannot define living things
Biodiversity: the number and variety of organisms on Earth; about 1.7-1.8 million species described
Need for standardised naming because local names vary from place to place
Nomenclature: giving a correct scientific name to an organism
Identification: correctly describing an organism before naming it
ICBN for plants and ICZN for animals as the codes that govern scientific names
Binomial nomenclature proposed by Carolus Linnaeus: generic name + specific epithet
Rules of binomial names: Latin/latinised, italicised when printed or underlined separately when handwritten
Genus name starts with a capital letter; specific epithet with a small letter; author's name abbreviated after the epithet (e.g. Mangifera indica Linn.)
Classification: grouping organisms into convenient categories based on observable characters
Taxon: a group at any level of classification (e.g. plants, mammals, dogs)
Taxonomy: characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature together
Systematics: study of kinds and diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships (Latin 'systema')
Bases of modern taxonomic studies: external and internal structure, cell structure, development and ecology
Exercise type: write scientific names correctly following binomial rules
Taxonomic hierarchy: categories arranged in a step-like order from kingdom to species
Each category (rank) is a unit of classification and represents a taxon
Species: group of individuals with fundamental similarities; specific epithet examples (Panthera leo, P. tigris)
Genus: group of related species with more common characters (e.g. Panthera, Solanum)
Family: group of related genera (e.g. Felidae, Canidae, Solanaceae)
Order: assemblage of families with a few similar characters (e.g. Carnivora, Polymoniales)
Class: related orders (e.g. Mammalia, Dicotyledonae)
Phylum (animals) / Division (plants): related classes (e.g. Chordata)
Kingdom: highest category (Animalia, Plantae)
Number of shared characters decreases from species up to kingdom
Taxonomic classification of common organisms: housefly, man, mango, wheat
Exercise type: arrange categories in ascending/descending hierarchy
Exercise type: explain why a species is the basic unit and define a taxon
Exercise type: identify the correct classification of a given organism
Aristotle's early classification of plants (trees, shrubs, herbs) and animals (with/without red blood)
Linnaeus' two-kingdom system (Plantae and Animalia) and its shortcomings
R.H. Whittaker's five-kingdom classification (1969): Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia
Criteria used: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction, phylogenetic relationships
Comparison table of characteristics of the five kingdoms
Three-domain system idea (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) mentioned
Bacteria: most abundant microorganisms; shapes - coccus, bacillus, vibrio, spirillum
Nutritional diversity: autotrophic (photosynthetic, chemosynthetic) and heterotrophic bacteria
2.1.1 Archaebacteria: live in extreme habitats - halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens; distinct cell wall
Methanogens in ruminant guts produce methane (biogas)
2.1.2 Eubacteria: rigid cell wall, flagellum if motile
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae): chlorophyll a, colonial/filamentous, heterocysts fix nitrogen (Nostoc, Anabaena), form blooms
Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise inorganic compounds and recycle N, P, Fe, S
Heterotrophic bacteria as decomposers; uses (curd, antibiotics, N-fixation) and diseases (cholera, typhoid, tetanus, citrus canker)
Reproduction in bacteria by fission, spores, and DNA transfer (sexual-like)
Mycoplasma: lack a cell wall, smallest living cells, survive without oxygen, pathogenic
Single-celled eukaryotes; link between plants, animals and fungi; mostly aquatic
Chrysophytes: diatoms and desmids; siliceous walls; diatomaceous earth; chief producers in oceans
Dinoflagellates: marine photosynthetic, two flagella, cellulose plates; red tides (Gonyaulax) and toxins
Euglenoids: no cell wall, protein-rich pellicle, two flagella; mixotrophic (Euglena)
Slime moulds: saprophytic, plasmodium formation, fruiting bodies, resistant spores
Protozoans: heterotrophs - amoeboid (Amoeba, Entamoeba), flagellated (Trypanosoma), ciliated (Paramoecium), sporozoans (Plasmodium)
Heterotrophic, saprophytic/parasitic/symbiotic (lichens, mycorrhiza); uses (yeast, Penicillium) and diseases (rusts, smuts)
Body of hyphae forming mycelium; coenocytic hyphae; cell wall of chitin and polysaccharides
Reproduction: vegetative (fragmentation, fission, budding), asexual spores (conidia, sporangiospores, zoospores), sexual spores (oospores, ascospores, basidiospores)
Sexual cycle: plasmogamy, karyogamy, meiosis; dikaryon stage (n+n)
Phycomycetes: aseptate coenocytic mycelium; zoospores/aplanospores; Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo
Ascomycetes (sac fungi): septate mycelium, conidia, ascospores in asci/ascocarps; Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora, morels, truffles
Basidiomycetes: mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs; basidiospores on basidia; Agaricus, Ustilago, Puccinia
Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi): only asexual phase known; decomposers; Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma
Eukaryotic, chlorophyll-containing organisms; cellulose cell walls; includes algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms
Some partially heterotrophic plants: insectivorous (Venus fly trap, bladderwort) and parasites (Cuscuta)
Alternation of generations between haploid gametophyte and diploid sporophyte (brief mention)
Heterotrophic, multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; holozoic nutrition; glycogen/fat as reserve
Definite growth pattern, locomotion in most, sexual reproduction with embryological development
Viruses as non-cellular, obligate parasites; inert crystalline outside the host
Discovery: Pasteur's term, Ivanowsky (TMV, 1892), Beijerinek 'contagium vivum fluidum', Stanley crystallisation
Structure: nucleoprotein - genetic material (RNA or DNA) and protein coat (capsid of capsomeres)
Plant viruses usually ssRNA; animal viruses RNA or DNA; bacteriophages usually dsDNA
Viral diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza, AIDS; plant symptoms - mosaic, leaf curl, yellowing, stunting
Viroids: free RNA without protein coat (T.O. Diener, potato spindle tuber disease)
Prions: abnormally folded proteins causing BSE (mad cow disease) and CJD
Lichens: symbiosis of algae (phycobiont) and fungi (mycobiont); pollution indicators
Exercise type: compare kingdoms, list economic importance of bacteria/fungi, distinguish viruses from viroids
Artificial systems based on few vegetative/sexual characters (Linnaeus) and their limitations
Natural systems based on natural affinities and many characters (Bentham and Hooker)
Phylogenetic systems based on evolutionary relationships
Numerical taxonomy using computers and coded characters; cytotaxonomy (chromosome number/structure); chemotaxonomy (chemical constituents)
Chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, mostly aquatic autotrophs; forms from unicellular (Chlamydomonas) to colonial (Volvox) and filamentous (Ulothrix, Spirogyra)
Vegetative reproduction by fragmentation; asexual by zoospores
Sexual reproduction types: isogamy, anisogamy, oogamy with examples
Importance: half of global CO2 fixation, primary producers, food (Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum), algin, carrageen, agar, Chlorella as food supplement
3.1.1 Chlorophyceae (green algae): chlorophyll a and b, pyrenoids, starch storage, cellulose walls
3.1.2 Phaeophyceae (brown algae): chlorophyll a, c, fucoxanthin; laminarin and mannitol storage; holdfast, stipe, frond; Ectocarpus, Fucus
3.1.3 Rhodophyceae (red algae): r-phycoerythrin, floridean starch, deep-water growth; Polysiphonia, Gracilaria, Gelidium
Comparison table of the three algal classes (pigments, stored food, cell wall, flagella, habitat)
Amphibians of the plant kingdom; moist shady habitats; role in plant succession on rocks
Plant body thallus-like, rhizoids, no true roots/stems/leaves; main body is haploid gametophyte
Sex organs: antheridium (antherozoids) and archegonium (egg); water needed for fertilisation
Sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) attached to and dependent on gametophyte; spores formed by meiosis
Economic importance: food for herbivores, Sphagnum peat as fuel and packing material
3.2.1 Liverworts: thalloid (Marchantia); gemmae for asexual reproduction; dorsiventral thallus
3.2.2 Mosses: protonema and leafy stages; multicellular rhizoids; elaborate spore dispersal; Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum
First terrestrial plants with vascular tissues (xylem, phloem); horsetails and ferns
Main plant body is sporophyte with true root, stem and leaves (microphylls/megaphylls)
Sporangia on sporophylls; strobili/cones (Selaginella, Equisetum)
Prothallus: free-living gametophyte needing water for fertilisation
Homosporous vs heterosporous pteridophytes; heterospory as precursor to seed habit
Classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum), Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum)
Uses: medicinal, soil binders, ornamental
Naked-seeded plants: ovules not enclosed in ovary
Range of forms: Cycas (small), Sequoia (tallest tree); tap roots, coralloid roots (Cycas, N2-fixing cyanobacteria), mycorrhizal roots (Pinus)
Leaves: simple or compound; needle-like leaves with thick cuticle and sunken stomata to reduce water loss
Heterosporous: microsporangia on microsporophylls (male cones), megasporangia on megasporophylls (female cones)
Pollen grain development, pollination by air, pollen tube carrying male gametes to archegonia
Ovule: nucellus with integuments; female gametophyte bearing archegonia
Seeds develop from fertilised ovules and are not covered
Exercise type: compare bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms
Exercise type: list features distinguishing gymnosperms from angiosperms (summary-level only; Angiosperms section deleted)
Recap of plant groups in increasing complexity; angiosperms named only in passing (dedicated section and life-cycle/alternation-of-generation section deleted)
Exercise type: basis of classification of algae; ploidy of protonema, prothallus, spores etc.
Exercise type: give economic importance of algae and gymnosperms
Need for classification despite structural differences; common fundamental features used
4.1.1 Levels of organisation: cellular (sponges), tissue (coelenterates), organ (flatworms), organ-system (higher phyla)
Incomplete digestive system (single opening) vs complete (mouth and anus)
Open vs closed circulatory system
4.1.2 Symmetry: asymmetrical (sponges), radial (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms), bilateral (annelids, arthropods etc.)
4.1.3 Diploblastic (ectoderm, endoderm, mesoglea) vs triploblastic (with mesoderm) organisation
4.1.4 Coelom: coelomates, pseudocoelomates (aschelminthes) and acoelomates (platyhelminthes)
4.1.5 Segmentation: metameric segmentation (metamerism) in earthworm
4.1.6 Notochord: chordates vs non-chordates
Flowchart of broad classification of Animalia based on fundamental features

4.2.1 Phylum Porifera: sponges, cellular level, water canal system, ostia, osculum, choanocytes, spicules/spongin fibres, hermaphrodite, internal fertilisation, indirect development (Sycon, Spongilla, Euspongia)

4.2.2 Phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria): cnidoblasts/cnidocytes, tissue level, diploblastic, gastrovascular cavity, polyp and medusa, metagenesis (Obelia), corals (Physalia, Adamsia, Pennatula, Gorgonia, Meandrina, Aurelia)
4.2.3 Phylum Ctenophora: sea walnuts/comb jellies, eight ciliated comb plates, bioluminescence (Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana)
4.2.4 Phylum Platyhelminthes: flatworms, dorso-ventrally flattened, acoelomate, flame cells, hooks/suckers in parasites, regeneration in Planaria (Taenia, Fasciola)
4.2.5 Phylum Aschelminthes: roundworms, pseudocoelomate, complete alimentary canal, dioecious with sexual dimorphism (Ascaris, Wuchereria, Ancylostoma)
4.2.6 Phylum Annelida: metameric segmentation, true coelom, nephridia, closed circulation, parapodia in Nereis, dioecious/monoecious (Pheretima, Hirudinaria)

4.2.7 Phylum Arthropoda: largest phylum, chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, open circulation, Malpighian tubules, gills/book lungs/tracheae; economic, vector and living-fossil examples (Apis, Bombyx, Laccifer, Anopheles, Culex, Aedes, Locusta, Limulus)
4.2.8 Phylum Mollusca: second largest, soft body with calcareous shell, head-foot-visceral hump, mantle, radula (Pila, Pinctada, Sepia, Loligo, Octopus, Aplysia, Dentalium, Chaetopleura)
4.2.9 Phylum Echinodermata: spiny skin, radial adult symmetry, bilateral larva, water vascular system, no excretory system (Asterias, Echinus, Antedon, Cucumaria, Ophiura)
4.2.10 Phylum Hemichordata: worm-like, proboscis-collar-trunk, stomochord, earlier a sub-phylum (Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus)
Fundamental chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail
Comparison of chordates and non-chordates (table)
Subphyla Urochordata (notochord only in larval tail, e.g. Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum), Cephalochordata (life-long notochord, Branchiostoma) and Vertebrata
Vertebrates: notochord replaced by vertebral column; ventral muscular heart; kidneys; paired appendages
Division Agnatha (Cyclostomata) and Gnathostomata (superclasses Pisces and Tetrapoda)
Class Cyclostomata: jawless ectoparasites, circular sucking mouth, 6-15 gill slits, migrate to fresh water to spawn (Petromyzon, Myxine)
Class Chondrichthyes: cartilaginous fish, placoid scales, ventral mouth, no air bladder, claspers in males, electric organs/poison sting (Scoliodon, Pristis, Carcharodon, Trygon, Torpedo)
Class Osteichthyes: bony fish, operculum, cycloid/ctenoid scales, air bladder, mostly oviparous (Exocoetus, Hippocampus, Labeo, Catla, Clarias, Betta, Pterophyllum)
Class Amphibia: dual life, moist skin, tympanum, cloaca, three-chambered heart, external fertilisation (Bufo, Rana, Hyla, Salamandra, Ichthyophis)

Class Reptilia: creeping mode, dry cornified scaly skin, mostly three-chambered heart (four in crocodiles), snake moulting, internal fertilisation (Chelone, Testudo, Chameleon, Calotes, Crocodilus, Naja, Vipera)
Class Aves: feathers, beak, forelimbs as wings, pneumatic bones, crop and gizzard, four-chambered heart, warm-blooded (Corvus, Columba, Psittacula, Struthio, Pavo, Aptenodytes, Neophron)

Class Mammalia: mammary glands, hair, external pinnae, different types of teeth, four-chambered heart, viviparous (Ornithorhynchus oviparous, Macropus, Pteropus, Camelus, Macaca, Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Equus, Delphinus, Balaenoptera, Panthera)
Salient features of the various phyla summarised in a table

Exercise type: match animals with distinctive features (e.g. comb plates, cnidoblasts, water canal system)

Tap root system from radicle in dicots (mustard)
Fibrous root system in monocots (wheat) arising from the base of stem
Adventitious roots from parts other than radicle (grass, Monstera, banyan)

Stem as ascending axis from plumule; nodes, internodes, buds
Functions: spreading branches, conduction of water/minerals/photosynthates, storage, support, protection, vegetative propagation
Note: modifications of stem deleted
Leaf as lateral flattened structure borne at node with axillary bud; parts: leaf base, petiole, lamina; stipules; pulvinus in legumes
5.3.1 Venation: reticulate (dicots) vs parallel (monocots)
5.3.2 Types of leaves: simple vs compound; pinnately compound (neem) vs palmately compound (silk cotton)
5.3.3 Phyllotaxy: alternate (china rose, mustard), opposite (Calotropis, guava), whorled (Alstonia)
Note: modifications of leaves deleted
Inflorescence: arrangement of flowers on the floral axis; flower as modified shoot
Racemose inflorescence: main axis grows continuously; flowers in acropetal order
Cymose inflorescence: main axis ends in a flower; basipetal order
Flower as reproductive unit; thalamus/receptacle; four whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium
Bisexual vs unisexual flowers
Symmetry: actinomorphic (radial), zygomorphic (bilateral), asymmetric
Trimerous, tetramerous, pentamerous flowers; bracteate vs ebracteate
Position of ovary: hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior), epigynous (inferior)
5.5.1 Parts of a flower: calyx (gamosepalous/polysepalous)
Corolla shapes and aestivation: valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary (papilionaceous)
Androecium: stamen (filament, anther), staminode, epipetalous and epiphyllous stamens; monoadelphous, diadelphous, polyadelphous
Gynoecium: carpels (stigma, style, ovary), apocarpous vs syncarpous ovary
Placentation types: marginal, axile, parietal, free central, basal
Fruit as mature ripened ovary after fertilisation; parthenocarpic fruits form without fertilisation
Pericarp: epicarp, mesocarp, endocarp; drupe (mango, coconut) as example
Seed as fertilised ovule: seed coat and embryo (radicle, embryonal axis, cotyledons)
5.7.1 Structure of a dicotyledonous seed: testa, tegmen, hilum, micropyle, cotyledons, endospermic vs non-endospermic seeds (gram, pea, castor)
5.7.2 Structure of a monocotyledonous seed: endospermic seed, aleurone layer, scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza (maize)

Brief recall of meristematic and permanent tissues (simple: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma; complex: xylem, phloem) as building blocks (dedicated tissue section deleted)
Three tissue systems classified by location: epidermal, ground (fundamental), vascular (conducting)
6.1.1 Epidermal tissue system: epidermis, single layer of parenchymatous cells, cuticle (absent in roots)
Stomata: guard cells (bean-shaped in dicots, dumb-bell shaped in grasses), subsidiary cells, stomatal apparatus
Epidermal appendages: root hairs (unicellular) and trichomes (multicellular, secretory or not)
6.1.2 Ground tissue system: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles - cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays; mesophyll in leaves
6.1.3 Vascular tissue system: xylem and phloem forming vascular bundles
Open vascular bundles (with cambium, dicots) vs closed (no cambium, monocots)
Radial vascular bundles (roots) vs conjoint (stems, leaves); collateral arrangement with phloem outward
Exarch vs endarch protoxylem position

concepts.text: 6.2.1 Dicot root (sunflower): epiblema with root hairs, cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, conjunctive tissue, 2-4 xylem/phloem patches, small pith
Pericycle origin of lateral roots and vascular cambium
6.2.2 Monocot root: polyarch (more than six) xylem bundles, large well-developed pith, no secondary growth

6.2.3 Dicot stem: epidermis with cuticle and trichomes, hypodermis (collenchyma), cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, vascular bundles in a ring, conjoint open endarch, medullary rays, pith
6.2.4 Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered vascular bundles with bundle sheath, conjoint closed, water-containing cavities, no distinct pith/phloem parenchyma
6.2.5 Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: adaxial and abaxial epidermis, more stomata on lower side, palisade and spongy mesophyll, vascular bundles with bundle sheath in veins
6.2.6 Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: stomata on both surfaces, undifferentiated mesophyll, bulliform cells that roll leaves under water stress, parallel venation
Comparison table of dicot vs monocot root, stem and leaf
Diagram skills: T.S. of dicot root, monocot root, dicot stem, monocot stem, dicot and monocot leaf
Exercise type: identify a T.S. as root/stem, monocot/dicot from given features

Tissues organise into organs (e.g. stomach, lungs, heart, kidney) and organs into organ systems
Division of labour and the complexity of organ systems showing evolutionary trends
Morphology (external form) vs anatomy (internal organs) in animals
Common Indian frog Rana tigrina; cold-blooded (poikilotherms)
Camouflage/mimicry by colour change
Aestivation (summer sleep) and hibernation (winter sleep)
7.2.1 Morphology: moist slippery mucus-covered skin, dorsal olive green with spots, ventral pale yellow; absorbs water through skin
Body divided into head and trunk; no neck or tail; protruding eyes with nictitating membrane; tympanum
Forelimbs and hind limbs; webbed digits of hind limb for swimming; sexual dimorphism (vocal sacs, copulatory pad in males)
7.2.2 Anatomy: body cavity houses organ systems
Digestive system: short alimentary canal (carnivore), bilobed tongue, oesophagus, stomach, intestine, rectum, cloaca; liver (bile), gall bladder, pancreas
Respiration: cutaneous in water; pulmonary (lungs) and buccal cavity on land; skin breathing during aestivation/hibernation
Circulatory system: closed; three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle), sinus venosus, conus arteriosus; hepatic and renal portal systems; lymphatic system
Blood composition: plasma, RBCs (nucleated), WBCs, platelets
Excretory system: pair of kidneys, ureters, cloaca, urinary bladder; ureter acts as urinogenital duct in males; ureotelic
Control and coordination: neural and endocrine systems; endocrine glands of frog (pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal, pancreatic islets, adrenals, gonads)
Nervous system: CNS (brain and spinal cord), peripheral (10 pairs of cranial nerves) and autonomic; brain divided into fore-, mid- and hind-brain
Sense organs: touch (papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes), hearing (tympanum with internal ear)
Male reproductive organs: yellowish ovoid testes, vasa efferentia, Bidder's canal, urinogenital duct, cloaca
Female reproductive organs: ovaries, oviducts opening into cloaca; 2500-3000 ova laid at a time
External fertilisation in water; development through tadpole larva with metamorphosis
Usefulness of frogs: eat insects, maintain ecological balance (food chain link), legs eaten as food

Exercise type: describe skin's role in respiration and features showing adaptation to amphibious life
Cell as the fundamental structural and functional unit of life; unicellular vs multicellular organisms
Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw a live cell; Robert Brown discovered the nucleus
Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed the cell theory; Schwann noted the plasma membrane and cell wall
Rudolf Virchow: Omnis cellula-e cellula - new cells arise from pre-existing cells
Modern cell theory: all living organisms are made of cells and cell products; all cells arise from pre-existing cells
Cytoplasm as the main arena of cellular activities; nucleus with chromosomes in eukaryotes
Membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotes vs nucleoid in prokaryotes; ribosomes in both
Variation in cell size (Mycoplasma 0.3 um, bacteria 3-5 um, ostrich egg largest, nerve cells longest) and shape (disc, polygonal, columnar, cuboid, thread-like, irregular)
Bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma, PPLO; shapes bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum
Genomic DNA as single circular chromosome in nucleoid; plasmids carrying traits like antibiotic resistance
8.4.1 Cell envelope: glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule), cell wall, plasma membrane
Gram-positive vs Gram-negative bacteria based on Gram staining
Mesosome: infoldings of plasma membrane - wall formation, DNA replication, respiration, secretion; chromatophores in cyanobacteria
Flagella (filament, hook, basal body), pili and fimbriae and their roles
8.4.2 Ribosomes and inclusion bodies: 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S), polysomes; inclusion bodies (phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen, gas vacuoles)
Eukaryotes: protists, plants, animals, fungi; organised nucleus with nuclear envelope; locomotory and cytoskeletal structures
Differences between plant and animal cells (cell wall, plastids, large vacuole vs centrioles)
8.5.1 Cell membrane: lipid bilayer with proteins; fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972); peripheral vs integral proteins
Functions of membrane: transport, passive (diffusion, osmosis) and active transport (Na+/K+ pump)
8.5.2 Cell wall: algal and plant wall composition; primary wall, secondary wall, middle lamella (calcium pectate), plasmodesmata
8.5.3 Endomembrane system: ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles function in coordination
Endoplasmic reticulum: RER (ribosomes, protein synthesis and secretion) vs SER (lipid/steroid synthesis); luminal and extra-luminal compartments
Golgi apparatus (Camillo Golgi): cisternae, cis (forming) and trans (maturing) faces; packaging, glycoproteins and glycolipids formation
Lysosomes: hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH
Vacuoles: tonoplast, cell sap; contractile vacuole (osmoregulation, excretion), food vacuole in protists
8.5.4 Mitochondria: double membrane, cristae, matrix; aerobic respiration sites (powerhouse); own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes; divide by fission
8.5.5 Plastids: chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts (amyloplasts, elaioplasts, aleuroplasts)
Chloroplast structure: double membrane, stroma, thylakoids, grana, stroma lamellae; own DNA and 70S ribosomes
8.5.6 Ribosomes: George Palade; RNA and protein, no membrane; 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes; Svedberg unit meaning
8.5.7 Cytoskeleton: microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments - support, motility, shape
8.5.8 Cilia and flagella: axoneme with 9+2 arrangement, radial spokes, central sheath, basal body
8.5.9 Centrosome and centrioles: cartwheel organisation, 9 triplets, hub; form basal bodies and spindle apparatus
8.5.10 Nucleus: nuclear envelope with perinuclear space and pores, nucleoplasm, nucleolus (rRNA synthesis), chromatin
Chromosomes: centromere, kinetochore; metacentric, sub-metacentric, acrocentric, telocentric; satellites and secondary constriction
8.5.11 Microbodies: membrane-bound minute vesicles with enzymes in plant and animal cells

Red fibres (myoglobin-rich, many mitochondria, aerobic) vs white fibres (little myoglobin, anaerobic, abundant sarcoplasmic reticulum)
Bones and cartilage form the framework; 206 bones in adult human
Axial skeleton (80 bones): skull (22 bones - 8 cranial and 14 facial), hyoid, ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes)
Vertebral column: 26 serially arranged vertebrae - cervical (7), thoracic (12), lumbar (5), sacral (1 fused), coccygeal (1 fused); neural canal
Sternum and ribs: 12 pairs; true ribs (1-7 pairs), false/vertebrochondral ribs (8-10), floating ribs (11-12); rib cage

Appendicular skeleton (126 bones): forelimb bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals 8, metacarpals 5, phalanges 14) and hind limb bones (femur, tibia, fibula, tarsals 7, metatarsals 5, phalanges 14, patella)
Pectoral girdle (clavicle, scapula, glenoid cavity, acromion) and pelvic girdle (coxal bones - ilium, ischium, pubis; acetabulum; pubic symphysis)

Joints as points of contact between bones; act as fulcrum for force from muscles
Fibrous joints: immovable (skull sutures)
Cartilaginous joints: limited movement (between adjacent vertebrae)
Synovial joints: fluid-filled synovial cavity; ball and socket (humerus-pectoral girdle), hinge (knee), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (carpals), saddle (carpal-metacarpal of thumb)

concepts.text: Myasthenia gravis: autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular junction causing fatigue, weakness and paralysis
Muscular dystrophy: progressive genetic degeneration of skeletal muscle
Tetany: rapid spasms due to low Ca2+ in body fluid
Arthritis (joint inflammation); osteoporosis (age-related reduced bone mass, low oestrogen); gout (uric acid crystal accumulation in joints)

Neurons as basic units that detect, receive and transmit stimuli
Evolutionary range: network of neurons in Hydra; ganglia in insects; well-developed brain in vertebrates
Central neural system (CNS: brain and spinal cord) and peripheral neural system (PNS: cranial and spinal nerves)
Afferent fibres carry impulses to CNS; efferent fibres from CNS to effectors
PNS divisions: somatic neural system (to skeletal muscles) and autonomic neural system (to involuntary organs and smooth muscles)
Autonomic system divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic; visceral nervous system concept

sections.name: 18.3 Neuron as Structural and Functional Unit of Neural System

concepts.text: Neuron structure: cell body with Nissl's granules, dendrites, axon ending in synaptic knobs with synaptic vesicles (neurotransmitters)
Types by processes: multipolar (cerebral cortex), bipolar (retina), unipolar (embryonic stage)
Myelinated axons (Schwann cell sheath, nodes of Ranvier; spinal/cranial nerves) vs non-myelinated axons (autonomic and somatic systems)
18.3.1 Generation and conduction of nerve impulse: polarised membrane at rest - ion channels selectively permeable; high K+ inside, high Na+ outside
Sodium-potassium pump: 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in; resting potential
Stimulus increases Na+ permeability: depolarisation and action potential (nerve impulse)
Impulse conduction along axon by local currents; repolarisation by K+ efflux restores resting potential
18.3.2 Transmission of impulses: synapse formed by pre- and post-synaptic membranes with synaptic cleft
Electrical synapses: direct current flow, faster, rare in our system
Chemical synapses: neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine) released by exocytosis, bind receptors, open ion channels causing excitatory or inhibitory potentials
Brain as central information processing organ; protected by cranium and meninges (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater)
18.4.1 Forebrain: cerebrum with left and right hemispheres joined by corpus callosum; cerebral cortex (grey matter) with sensory, motor and association areas; white matter
Thalamus as coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling; hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, and secretes neurohormones
Limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus) regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions and motivation
18.4.2 Midbrain: between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons; cerebral aqueduct; corpora quadrigemina
18.4.3 Hindbrain: pons, cerebellum (large surface for neurons), medulla (controls respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, gastric secretions)
Brain stem = midbrain + pons + medulla oblongata

Endocrine (ductless) glands secrete hormones into blood
Modern definition: hormones are non-nutrient chemicals acting as intercellular messengers in trace amounts
Invertebrates have simple endocrine systems; vertebrates use many chemicals as hormones
Endocrine glands and hormone-producing tissues/cells located throughout the body; map of major glands
19.2.1 The hypothalamus: neurosecretory cells (nuclei) producing releasing (e.g. GnRH) and inhibiting (e.g. somatostatin) hormones; hypophyseal portal system
19.2.2 The pituitary gland: in sella turcica; adenohypophysis (pars distalis, pars intermedia) and neurohypophysis (pars nervosa)
Pars distalis hormones: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH; pars intermedia: MSH
GH disorders: gigantism, dwarfism, acromegaly; prolactin for mammary glands; TSH, ACTH roles; LH and FSH (gonadotrophins) in males and females
Neurohypophysis stores and releases oxytocin (smooth muscle contraction, childbirth, milk ejection) and vasopressin/ADH (water reabsorption); diabetes insipidus
19.2.3 The pineal gland: melatonin - diurnal (24 h) rhythm, sleep-wake cycle, body temperature, metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle, defence
19.2.4 Thyroid gland: two lobes joined by isthmus; follicles; thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); iodine needed
Thyroid disorders: hypothyroidism and goitre (iodine deficiency), cretinism, hyperthyroidism, exophthalmic goitre (Graves' disease); effects on BMR, RBC formation, metabolism
Thyrocalcitonin (TCT) regulates blood calcium levels
19.2.5 Parathyroid gland: four glands on back of thyroid; parathyroid hormone (PTH) is hypercalcaemic - bone resorption, Ca2+ reabsorption in tubules, absorption from food
19.2.6 Thymus: on dorsal side of heart and aorta; thymosins for T-lymphocyte differentiation (cell-mediated immunity) and antibodies (humoral immunity); degenerates with age
19.2.7 Adrenal gland: one on each kidney; adrenal medulla secretes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (catecholamines) - emergency hormones (fight or flight)
Adrenal cortex: zona reticularis, zona fasciculata, zona glomerulosa; glucocorticoids (cortisol) - gluconeogenesis, anti-inflammatory, immune suppression
Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) for Na+/water reabsorption and K+ excretion; androgenic steroids; Addison's disease from hyposecretion
19.2.8 Pancreas: composite gland; islets of Langerhans with alpha cells (glucagon, hyperglycaemic) and beta cells (insulin, hypoglycaemic)
Glucagon: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis; insulin: cellular glucose uptake, glycogenesis; diabetes mellitus (hyperglycaemia, ketone bodies) treated with insulin
19.2.9 Testis: Leydig (interstitial) cells secrete androgens (testosterone) - male accessory organs, spermatogenesis, secondary sex characters, libido, anabolic effects
19.2.10 Ovary: oestrogen from growing follicles (female secondary sex characters, mammary gland development) and progesterone from corpus luteum (supports pregnancy, milk-secreting alveoli)

sections.name: 19.3 Hormones of Heart, Kidney and Gastrointestinal Tract

concepts.text: Atrial natriuretic factor (ANF) from atrial wall lowers blood pressure by dilating blood vessels
Erythropoietin from juxtaglomerular cells of kidney stimulates RBC formation

GI tract hormones: gastrin (gastric glands - HCl and pepsinogen), secretin (exocrine pancreas - water and bicarbonate), cholecystokinin (pancreatic enzymes and bile), gastric inhibitory peptide (inhibits gastric secretion and motility)
Growth factors from non-endocrine tissues for normal growth and tissue repair
Hormones bind specific hormone receptors on target tissues: membrane-bound receptors vs intracellular (nuclear) receptors
Hormone-receptor complex causes biochemical changes in target tissue

Chemical classes: peptide/polypeptide/protein hormones (insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones), steroids (cortisol, testosterone, oestradiol, progesterone), iodothyronines (thyroid hormones), amino-acid derivatives (epinephrine)
Membrane-receptor hormones (non-entry) act via second messengers (cyclic AMP, IP3, Ca2+) to regulate metabolism
Intracellular-receptor hormones (steroids, iodothyronines) regulate gene expression/chromosome function, causing physiological and developmental effects
